newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean leader sacks top aides to defuse crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean leader sacks top aides to defuse crisis.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam kicked off a sweeping administration reshuffle on Friday aimed at restoring political credibility badly damaged by a loans scandal.
Kim replaced his chief secretary and three other top advisers responsible for political, economic and general affairs, a presidential spokesman said.
"This is the start of a major reshuffle in the government and the ruling party," he said. "The cabinet reshuffle is expected early next week."
Separately, Kim sacked the country's second ranking intelligence officer. No reason was given.

Opposition politicians have alleged that Kim Ki-sup, deputy chief of the Agency for National Security Planning, was close to the president's second son, widely referred to as South Korea's "crown prince".
Kim Young-sam banished his son, Hyun-chul, from public life after he was questioned by state prosecutors in connection with the loans scandal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Hyun-chul was cleared of wrongdoing, but the president said he was ashamed that his son was embroiled in the controversy.
Former home affairs minister Kim Yong-tae, who served four terms in parliament, is to succeed Kim Kwang-il as chief of staff at the presidential Blue House.

All members of Kim Young-sam's Blue House inner circle, the entire cabinet and ruling New Korea Party leaders had offered to step down after the president apologised over the scandal on Tuesday, the fourth anniversary of his inauguration.
Kim Young-sam took ultimate responsibility for the loans-for-kickbacks scandal.
The chief Blue House political officer, Lee Won-jong, was replaced by Kang In-sup, a former member of parliament and an ex-journalist.
His counterpart in charge of economic affairs, Lee Suk-chae, stepped down in favour of Kim In-ho, current head of the Fair Trade Commission.
The president met former finance minister Kim Mahn-je on Thursday, sparking speculation that he would be named as new premier, replacing Lee Soo-sung.
Another person tipped as a candidate for premier is Koh Kun, who held ministerial portfolios for transport, agriculture and home affairs in the 1980s. He is now a university dean.
Domestic media said any new premier was likely to be an economic expert in view of the slowing economy.

South Korea's presidential system concentrates power in the Blue House and Kim's aides have wielded great influence over policy. The chief presidential secretary's job is described by some newspapers as "vice presidency behind the facade".

Political analysts said the president appeared to be fighting to regain his credibility and avoid being labelled a lame duck during his last year in office. He is constitutionally barred from seeking a second term.

The Hanbo scandal highlighted the failure of President Kim's much vaunted anti-corruption drive, and he promised on Tuesday to heed criticism that his close associates were incapable of carrying through reforms.

Prosecutors said banks, under pressure from politicians, had offered huge loans in return for kickbacks from Hanbo, which managed to pile up $5.8 billion in debts before it was declared insolvent on January 23.

Three of President Kim's senior aides, including a cabinet minister, have been arrested on bribery charges over the scandal. Kim, a former dissident who battled previous military rulers, took power in 1993 vowing a clean society.
Political analysts said the cabinet reshuffle is likely to be announced after the current parliamentary interpellation session ends on Monday.
